title: Memory Management
summary: Virtual memory from first principles: address spaces, paging and x86-64 page tables, the TLB, page faults and copy-on-write, page replacement, malloc and kernel allocators, and debugging memory on real Linux systems and containers.

lessons.title: Virtual addresses and private memory
lessons.summary: A pointer names a location in a process address space, rather than directly identifying installed RAM.
lessons.body:
Run two copies of the same program and print the address of a global variable in each. With a non-PIE executable, disabled address randomization, or a parent/child created by `fork`, the address can match while each process has its own value. Independent ASLR-enabled PIE executions generally choose different layouts. Both statements are true because the address the program sees is interpreted through a mapping rather than directly identifying a physical RAM location.

That illusion is **virtual memory**. Every process gets its own private **address space**: a huge, clean range of addresses that looks as if it belongs to that process alone. The operating system and the hardware quietly map those addresses onto real memory.

This unit introduces that mapping model. The following units explain isolation, early base-and-bounds and segmentation schemes, then paging.

## Physical and virtual addresses

A **physical address** identifies a location in the machine's physical address space, which can include RAM, device mappings and holes. 16 GiB contains 17,179,869,184 bytes, but installed RAM need not occupy one contiguous range of physical addresses.

A **virtual address** is what a program uses: every pointer in C, every instruction fetch, every stack push. With four-level x86-64 paging, the lower canonical half spans 128 TiB; five-level paging expands it to 64 PiB. The card below shows the corresponding powers of two. Actual usable mappings are constrained by kernel policy and reserved regions.

Those sizes all come from one rule: an address is a binary number, and every extra bit doubles how many different bytes it can name. Memory sizes are therefore powers of two, and the binary units (KiB, MiB, GiB and so on) are powers of two as well:

```formula
N = 2^n
16 GiB = 2^4 × 2^30 B = 2^34 B
2^47 B = 2^7 × 2^40 B = 128 TiB
2^56 B = 2^6 × 2^50 B = 64 PiB
where
N: the number of different bytes an address can name, which is the size of the address space in bytes
n: the number of bits in the address
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together; for example 2^10 = 1,024 and 2^4 = 16. Multiplying powers of two adds their exponents: 2^4 × 2^30 = 2^34
B: byte, 8 bits; each address names one byte
GiB: gibibyte, 2^30 bytes (1,073,741,824 B)
TiB: tebibyte, 2^40 bytes, or 1,024 GiB
PiB: pebibyte, 2^50 bytes, or 1,024 TiB
In words: n address bits can name 2^n bytes, so 34 bits cover 16 GiB, the 47 bits of the lower canonical half cover 128 TiB, and 56 bits cover 64 PiB.
```

For example, a 32-bit byte address can name 4 GiB, by the same rule: that is the address-space limit, before any user/kernel split or reserved mappings. The formula counts addresses, not memory: it says nothing about how much RAM is actually installed or mapped.

On every single memory access, a piece of hardware in the CPU called the **memory management unit (MMU)** translates the virtual address into a physical one, using tables the OS set up.

```
 process A          MMU           RAM
 0x4000 ----+                +---------+
            +--> translate ->| frame 7 |
 process B  |    (A's map)   |  ...    |
 0x4000 ----+--> translate ->| frame 2 |
                 (B's map)   +---------+
```

Same virtual address, different physical location, because each process has its own map.

## Key takeaways
- A pointer names a location in a process address space, rather than directly identifying installed RAM.
- Address-bit counts describe possible addresses; mappings and RAM capacity are separate limits.

questions.prompt: Two processes use the same virtual address for a global variable. Must those addresses refer to the same physical byte?

options.text: Yes, equal pointer values always identify the same RAM byte.
options.explanation: A pointer value is interpreted within an address space; equal numeric addresses can use different mappings.

options.text: No, their separate address-space mappings can choose different backing.
options.explanation: The MMU uses the relevant process mapping, so identical virtual numbers can translate to distinct physical locations.

options.text: No, because a virtual address is never translated into a physical address.
options.explanation: Ordinary accesses do use translation; separation comes from the mapping context, rather than the absence of translation.

questions.workedExample: Take virtual address 0x4000 in both processes. The diagram maps that address through process A’s table to frame 7 and through process B’s table to frame 2. Equal virtual numbers therefore do not imply shared physical storage. Explicit shared mappings can arrange sharing instead.

lessons.title: Why a forked child has its own values
lessons.summary: Relocation, isolation and sparse capacity motivate virtual memory.

options.text: Two different addresses; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 2
options.explanation: The child's write cannot reach the parent's memory, and the addresses will match because the child's address space is a copy of the parent's.

options.text: The same address twice; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 2
options.explanation: This assumes that the same virtual address means the same physical memory. Each process has its own mapping, so the child's write is invisible to the parent.

options.text: The same address twice; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 1
options.explanation: Correct. The child's address space is a copy of the parent's, so `&x` is the same virtual address, but it maps to a separate physical frame once the child writes.

options.text: Two different addresses; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 1
options.explanation: The values are right, but the addresses are the same: fork copies the address space layout exactly, including ASLR offsets.

questions.workedExample:
1. `fork()` creates a child whose address space is a duplicate of the parent's: the same regions at the same virtual addresses.
2. So `&x` is identical in both, for example `0x55e4c3a1b010`.
3. The child runs `x = 2;`. That write goes through the *child's* page tables to the child's copy of the page.
4. The parent waits, then reads `x` through its own page tables and gets its own copy, still 1.

```
c 0x55e4c3a1b010 2
p 0x55e4c3a1b010 1
```

The lesson: a virtual address is only meaningful inside one address space.

questions.prompt: Which problems does virtual memory solve for a multiprogrammed OS? Select all that apply.

options.text: Relocation: a program can run wherever it is placed in RAM without rewriting its pointers
options.explanation: Correct. Each process uses its own virtual addresses, and the MMU maps them to wherever the OS put the data.

options.text: Protection: ordinary accesses cannot reach another process's private memory without an authorized mapping or access mechanism
options.explanation: Correct. A process can only reach physical memory that its own tables map, and kernel pages are supervisor-only.

options.text: Speed: memory accesses become faster than with physical addressing
options.explanation: Wrong. Translation adds work to every access; the TLB exists to make that overhead small, not negative.

options.text: Sharing: one copy of a library's code can be mapped into many processes
options.explanation: Correct. Several address spaces can map the same physical frames, typically read-only for code.

options.text: It removes the need for CPU caches
options.explanation: Wrong. Caches address the speed gap between the core and DRAM, an entirely separate problem from translation.

questions.workedExample: Virtual memory supports relocation, isolation and deliberate sharing through per-address-space mappings and permissions. Programs need not start at address zero. Translation has implementation cost; it is not a general promise of faster access. Caches remain useful and their indexing/tagging design interacts with translation. Shared code pages may be reused while process-private data remains separate.

lessons.title: Reading a Linux address-space layout
lessons.summary: Canonical-address rules and mapping permissions constrain usable pointers.
lessons.body:
## What an address space looks like

A typical Linux x86-64 process maps selected regions of a much larger address range. This schematic assumes four-level paging; real layouts and mappings vary:

```
 0x7fff_ffff_ffff  lower canonical limit
 +-----------------+
 | stack           |  grows down
 |      ...        |
 | mmap region     |  libraries, mmap()
 |      ...        |
 | heap            |  grows up (brk)
 | .bss / .data    |  globals
 | .text           |  code, read-only
 +-----------------+
 0x0000_0000_0000  (normally unmapped)
```

You can see the real map of any process in `/proc/<pid>/maps`. Each line shows a range, its permissions (`r-xp` for code, `rw-p` for data) and what backs it (a file or nothing).

Points worth knowing:

- **Page 0 is normally left unmapped** to catch null-address accesses. Minimum-mapping policy and privileges can allow exceptions; a C null-pointer dereference is undefined behavior, not a portable promise of SIGSEGV.
- **ASLR** randomizes selected mappings when enabled; relocating executable code requires a suitable PIE executable. It makes address prediction harder, not impossible. `fork` preserves the parent's layout, including any randomized addresses.
- For ordinary x86-64 addresses with address-tag masking disabled, the address must be a **canonical address**: with 4-level paging, bits 63 to 47 must all be equal. Linux gives the lower half (0 to `0x00007fffffffffff`) to user space and keeps the upper half for the kernel.
- **Traditionally, kernel mappings appear in each process's page tables**, but its pages are marked supervisor-only, so user code gets a fault if it touches them. (After the 2018 Meltdown attack showed CPUs could leak that data speculatively, Linux added *kernel page-table isolation*, which unmaps most of the kernel while user code runs.)

## Pitfalls and misconceptions

- **"A pointer is a RAM address."** Not in user space. A pointer is meaningful only inside its own address space; passing its numeric value does not establish access in another process. Shared layouts can make pointers meaningful across processes; offsets within shared mappings are often more robust.
- **"Virtual memory means swap."** Swap is one feature built on virtual memory. Virtual memory is the translation layer, and it is in use on every access even on a phone with no swap at all.
- **"A big address space costs RAM."** The address space is mostly empty. Mappings can consume metadata and overcommit-accounting budget before resident pages are touched; resident backing, page tables and shared-page accounting also matter.

## Key takeaways
- Canonical-address rules and mapping permissions constrain usable pointers.
- ASLR changes selected layouts; KPTI separates reduced user and full kernel views.
- Passing a pointer value does not arrange access to another process’s memory.

## Further reading
- [OSTEP: The Abstraction: Address Spaces (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-intro.pdf)
- [OSTEP: Address Translation (base and bounds) (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-mechanism.pdf)
- [OSTEP: Segmentation (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-segmentation.pdf)
- [Virtual memory — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_memory)
- [Memory segmentation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_segmentation)
- [Address space layout randomization — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Address_space_layout_randomization)
- [Kernel page-table isolation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_page-table_isolation)

questions.prompt: Why do ordinary Linux processes normally leave virtual page 0 unmapped (for example, addresses 0–4095 with 4 KiB pages)? Consider an actual user-mode access instruction; portable C null-pointer dereference is undefined behaviour.

options.text: Because the BIOS interrupt table lives at physical address 0
options.explanation: That was true on real-mode PCs for *physical* address 0. Virtual page 0 could map to any frame; Linux leaves it unmapped for a different reason.

options.text: So an actual access to a null or small unmapped address faults instead of reading or corrupting mapped memory
options.explanation: Correct. A NULL dereference becomes a clean SIGSEGV, and there is also a `vm.mmap_min_addr` setting that stops processes mapping low pages, which blocks a class of kernel exploits.

options.text: Because the kernel's code is mapped there
options.explanation: On x86-64 Linux the kernel lives in the upper (negative) half of the address space, not at 0.

options.text: To save RAM, since page 0 would be wasted
options.explanation: An unmapped page costs no RAM whether it is at 0 or anywhere else; the choice of page 0 is about catching bugs.

questions.workedExample: On the stated Linux ABI a null pointer uses address zero. If generated code accesses that unmapped address, hardware faults and Linux normally delivers SIGSEGV. The C language itself makes null-pointer dereference undefined behavior. vm.mmap_min_addr restricts low mappings subject to configuration, capabilities and security policy; privileged exceptions exist. Low-mapping restrictions also mitigate some kernel null-dereference exploits.

questions.prompt: On x86-64 with 4-level paging (48-bit virtual addresses), with address-tag masking disabled, which of these ordinary linear addresses is **non-canonical**, so that using it raises a fault even before any page table is consulted?

options.text: `0x00007fffffffffff`
options.explanation: Canonical. Bits 63 to 47 are all 0. This is the highest user-space address on Linux.
Canonical. Bits 63 to 47 are all 1. This is the bottom of the kernel half.
Correct. Bit 47 is 1 but bits 63 to 48 are 0. They must all equal bit 47, so this address lies in the non-canonical 'hole'.

options.text: `0xffffffffffffffff`
options.explanation: Canonical. Every bit is 1, so bits 63 to 47 agree; this is the last byte of the kernel half.

questions.workedExample:
1. With 48-bit addressing, only 48 bits are translated. The rule is that bits 63 to 48 must be **copies of bit 47** (sign-extension).
2. That splits the space into two halves:

```
0x0000_0000_0000_0000
  .. 0x0000_7fff_ffff_ffff  user
(hole: non-canonical)
0xffff_8000_0000_0000
  .. 0xffff_ffff_ffff_ffff  kernel
```

3. `0x0000800000000000` has bit 47 = 1 and bits 63 to 48 = 0, which is inconsistent, so it is in the hole.
4. An ordinary non-stack memory access to this non-canonical address raises a general-protection fault; stack references can instead raise a stack-segment fault. The hole exists so that future CPUs can translate more bits (5-level paging uses 57) without old software abusing the spare bits.

questions.prompt: Assume a conventional 64-bit Linux process and ordinary generated memory-access instructions. Process A allocates a struct with malloc, then writes the raw pointer value (8 bytes) into a pipe. Process B, an unrelated program, reads those 8 bytes, casts them to a pointer, and dereferences it. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: B reads A's struct, because the pointer is a physical RAM address
options.explanation: User-space pointers are virtual. B's MMU translates them with B's page tables, which don't include A's heap.

options.text: B reads A's struct, because both processes share one heap
options.explanation: Each process has its own heap. Only explicitly shared mappings (for example `mmap` with `MAP_SHARED`, or System V shared memory) are visible to both.

options.text: The kernel translates the pointer for B automatically when it passes through the pipe
options.explanation: Pipes copy bytes; they do not interpret or translate them.

options.text: B either segfaults (the address is unmapped in B) or silently reads unrelated data of its own
options.explanation: Correct. The value is just a number in B's address space: either nothing is mapped there (SIGSEGV) or something of B's is, and B reads that instead.

questions.workedExample: A raw pointer value names an address in A's mapping. Sending bytes through a pipe does not grant B access or relocate the pointer. B may fault on an unmapped/protected address or access unrelated mapped storage; portable C provides no defined cross-process dereference guarantee. To share data, establish a shared mapping and communicate offsets or identifiers with a defined representation and synchronization protocol.

questions.prompt: On x86-64 Linux, why did traditional process page tables include supervisor-only kernel mappings, and what does enabled kernel page-table isolation (KPTI) change?

options.text: So user code can call kernel functions directly; KPTI made these calls go through the syscall instruction
options.explanation: User code could never call kernel functions directly: kernel pages are supervisor-only and fault from user mode.

options.text: So system calls and interrupts can reach supervisor-only kernel mappings without changing the page-table root; KPTI removes most of those mappings during user execution and switches views when crossing between user and kernel execution
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping the kernel mapped avoids a CR3 switch per syscall. Meltdown let user code speculatively read supervisor-only pages, so KPTI uses separate user tables with only a small trampoline mapped.

options.text: To save RAM by sharing kernel memory; KPTI duplicated the kernel per process
options.explanation: KPTI maintains separate user/kernel page-table views with some shared structures and additional tables. It does not duplicate the kernel's code/data per process.

options.text: Because 64-bit CPUs require it; KPTI moved the kernel to the lower half
options.explanation: No architecture requirement forces this layout, and KPTI didn't move the kernel; it changed what is mapped while user code runs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Before KPTI: each process's page tables include the kernel's mappings, marked supervisor-only (the U/S bit clear). A syscall changes the privilege level but **not** CR3, so no page-table switch and no TLB flush.
2. Protection relied on the permission check: user-mode access to those pages faults.
3. **Meltdown** (2018) showed that on many Intel CPUs the data could be loaded speculatively *before* the fault, then leaked through cache timing.
4. **KPTI**: while in user mode, the active page tables map only kernel mappings needed for entry/exit and related CPU structures. On entry from user mode, the kernel switches CR3 to the full tables, and back on return.
5. Cost: extra CR3 writes and potential TLB misses on every kernel crossing. PCIDs, covered in the later translation-cache units, can reduce refill work by retaining tagged translations when invalidation rules permit.

lessons.title: Translating with a base and a bound
lessons.summary: Check the virtual offset against the region size before adding its physical base.
lessons.body:
## Base and bounds

The simplest hardware translation, used on machines in the 1960s, is **base and bounds** (also called dynamic relocation). The CPU has two registers per running process:

- the **base register**: where the process's memory starts in physical RAM;
- the **bounds register** (or limit register): how big it is.

On every access the hardware does two things: a check (is the address inside the process's region?) and an add (where does the region start in RAM?). As a formula:

```formula
PA = VA + base   for 0 ≤ VA < bounds
where
PA: the physical address: the byte's real location in RAM
VA: the virtual address the program used, counted from 0 at the start of the process's own space
base: the base register: the physical address where the process's region starts
bounds: the bounds register: the size of the region in bytes, so the legal virtual addresses run from 0 to bounds − 1
≤: less than or equal to
<: strictly less than
In words: every legal virtual address is moved up by the base; an address at or beyond the bounds is illegal, and the hardware raises a fault instead of translating it.
```

The same logic as hardware pseudocode:

The following Python fragment models nonnegative, width-limited addresses; the surrounding simulator supplies the registers and a fault exception.

```python
# Reject offsets outside the region.
if virtual >= bounds:
    raise fault        # protection
physical = virtual + base
```

A worked example: a process is loaded at physical 32 KiB (a base of 32,768) with a bounds of 16 KiB (16,384 bytes).

```formula
VA = 3,000 < 16,384 = bounds
PA = VA + base
PA = 3,000 + 32,768 = 35,768
where
VA: the virtual address the program used; here byte 3,000
bounds: the bounds register, the size of the region; here 16,384 bytes (16 KiB)
PA: the physical address the hardware actually accesses
base: the base register; here 32,768 (32 KiB)
In words: virtual 3,000 is inside the 16 KiB region, so the hardware adds the 32 KiB base and the access goes to physical byte 35,768.
```

Virtual 20,000 is at or above 16,384, so the hardware raises a fault instead; an unhandled illegal access normally terminates the process. The scheme assumes the process's whole region is one contiguous block of RAM, which is where its weaknesses come from.

On a context switch, the OS saves one process's base and bounds and loads the next. Only the kernel may change these registers; otherwise a process could simply point its base at someone else's memory.

Base and bounds gives relocation and protection cheaply, but it has two serious flaws:

- **Wasted space inside the process.** The whole address space must be contiguous in RAM, including the unused gap between heap and stack. A process with a large virtual range but little actual data still reserves the lot.
- **External fragmentation.** As processes of different sizes come and go, free RAM ends up as scattered holes. You may have 100 MiB free in total but no single hole big enough for a 20 MiB process.

## Key takeaways
- Check the virtual offset against the region size before adding its physical base.
- A single contiguous process region wastes gaps and suffers external fragmentation.

## Further reading
- [OSTEP: The Abstraction: Address Spaces (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-intro.pdf)
- [OSTEP: Address Translation (base and bounds) (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-mechanism.pdf)
- [OSTEP: Segmentation (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-segmentation.pdf)
- [Virtual memory — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_memory)
- [Memory segmentation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_segmentation)
- [Address space layout randomization — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Address_space_layout_randomization)
- [Kernel page-table isolation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_page-table_isolation)

questions.prompt: A process runs under base-and-bounds translation with a **base of 40,000** and a **bounds of 8,000**. The program loads from virtual address **5,000**. Which physical address is accessed?

options.explanation: That is the virtual address. Under base and bounds the hardware always adds the base, so the program never sees its physical location.
Correct. 5,000 is less than the bounds of 8,000, so the access is legal, and the physical address is 5,000 + 40,000 = 45,000.
This adds the bounds to the base. The bounds is only used for the limit check, not in the address calculation.

options.text: It faults, because 5,000 is less than the base
options.explanation: The check compares the *virtual* address with the bounds, not with the base. Virtual addresses start at 0 for every process.

questions.workedExample:
Base and bounds does two things on every access: a check against the bounds, then an add of the base.

```formula
VA = 5,000 < 8,000 = bounds
PA = VA + base
PA = 5,000 + 40,000 = 45,000
where
VA: the virtual address the program used; here 5,000
bounds: the bounds register, the size of the region in bytes; here 8,000, so legal virtual addresses are 0 to 7,999
<: strictly less than
PA: the physical address actually accessed
base: the base register, where the region starts in physical memory; here 40,000
In words: 5,000 passes the bounds check, so the hardware adds the base and the access goes to physical 45,000.
```

The process's legal physical range is therefore 40,000 to 47,999. It can never reach anything outside that range, which is how the scheme provides protection.

questions.prompt: A process has a **base of 100,000** and a **bounds of 8,000**. It accesses virtual address **8,000**. What happens?

options.text: Physical address 108,000 is accessed
options.explanation: This is an off-by-one error. Legal virtual addresses are 0 to 7,999 (one less than the bounds), so 8,000 is one past the end.

options.text: Physical address 8,000 is accessed
options.explanation: Base and bounds always adds the base; physical address 8,000 might belong to the kernel or another process.

options.text: The hardware raises a fault and the OS typically kills the process
options.explanation: Correct. The hardware checks that the virtual address is less than the bounds. 8,000 is not less than 8,000, so the access is out of range.

options.text: The OS automatically grows the bounds to 8,001
options.explanation: The hardware faults; it does not automatically extend the region. The OS could grow in place if sufficient adjacent physical space were available, otherwise relocation or failure may be needed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Bounds is the **size** of the address space: 8,000 bytes means virtual addresses 0 to 7,999.
2. The hardware checks that the virtual address is strictly less than the bounds:

```formula
VA_max = bounds − 1 = 8,000 − 1 = 7,999
VA = 8,000 > VA_max
where
VA_max: the highest legal virtual address
bounds: the bounds register, the size of the region in bytes; here 8,000
VA: the virtual address accessed; here 8,000
>: greater than
In words: a region of 8,000 bytes covers addresses 0 to 7,999, so address 8,000 is one past the end.
```

3. The check fails, so the MMU raises an exception before any memory is touched.
4. The OS's handler sees an illegal access by a user process and terminates it (the ancestor of today's SIGSEGV).

Off-by-one at the boundary is a classic exam pitfall, so always check whether the limit is a size or a last valid address. On real hardware it varies; in this model it is the size.

lessons.title: Segments, sharing and fragmented holes
lessons.summary: Segment bits select a base and a limit; the remaining bits select an offset.
lessons.body:
## Segmentation

**Segmentation** generalises base and bounds: instead of one pair per process, there is one pair per logical **segment** (code, heap, stack and so on). Each segment can be placed anywhere in RAM independently, and the gap between heap and stack costs nothing.

The hardware needs to know which segment an address belongs to. One classic approach uses the top bits of the virtual address as a segment number and the rest as an offset (how far into the segment). With a 12-bit offset:

```formula
seg = ⌊VA / 2^12⌋
off = VA mod 2^12
PA = base_seg + off   for off < size_seg
where
VA: the virtual address the program used
seg: the segment number, which is the top bits of VA
off: the offset inside the segment, which is the low 12 bits of VA
2^12: 4,096 (0x1000 in hexadecimal); dividing by it strips off the 12 offset bits
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after division; for example 13 mod 5 = 3
base_seg: the base of segment number seg: where it starts in physical memory, read from the segment table
size_seg: the size of segment number seg in bytes, also from the segment table
PA: the physical address
In words: the top bits choose a row of the segment table, the low bits say how far into that segment, and the hardware adds the offset to that row's base after checking that it fits inside the segment.
```

> [!example] Segment translation
> A toy machine has 14-bit virtual addresses. The top 2 bits pick the segment and the low 12 bits are the offset.
>
> | Seg | Name | Base | Size |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 00 | code | 0x8000 | 2 KiB |
> | 01 | heap | 0xA000 | 3 KiB |
>
> Virtual 0x1068 is `01 0000 0110 1000` in binary: segment 01 (heap), offset 0x068 (104).

In hexadecimal, division by 4,096 (0x1000) drops the last three digits, so the segment and offset can be read off by eye:

```formula
seg = ⌊0x1068 / 2^12⌋ = 1
off = 0x1068 mod 2^12 = 0x068 = 104
off = 104 < 3,072 = size_1
PA = base_1 + off = 0xA000 + 0x068
PA = 0xA068
where
seg: the segment number; 1 (binary 01) is the heap
off: the offset inside the segment, in bytes
2^12: 4,096 (0x1000)
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after division
size_1: the heap segment's size, 3 KiB = 3,072 bytes
base_1: the heap segment's base, 0xA000
PA: the physical address
In words: address 0x1068 is 104 bytes into the heap, which is inside the 3 KiB segment, so it lands at 0xA000 + 0x068 = 0xA068.
```

Virtual 0x0C10 is segment 00 (code), offset 0xC10 (3,088). That exceeds the 2 KiB (2,048) code segment, so the access faults. This is where the term **segmentation fault** comes from; Linux uses SIGSEGV for invalid accesses; native x86-64 Linux primarily enforces process memory isolation through paging rather than segment bounds.

Segments also carry **protection bits**. Code can be marked read-and-execute only, which makes it safe to **share** one copy of a program's code between many processes.

But segments are still variable-sized and contiguous, so segmentation still suffers **external fragmentation**. The OS has to search for holes (best fit, first fit) or periodically **compact** memory by copying segments together, which is slow. A heap segment that needs to grow may also find no free space next to it.

## Key takeaways
- Segment bits select a base and a limit; the remaining bits select an offset.
- Read-only segments can share backing, but variable-sized contiguous segments still fragment.

## Further reading

questions.prompt:
A toy machine uses 14-bit virtual addresses. The top 2 bits select the segment; the low 12 bits are the offset.

| Seg | Base | Size |
|---|---|---|
| 00 code | 0x4000 | 0x800 |
| 01 heap | 0x9000 | 0xC00 |

What does virtual address **0x1A40** translate to?

options.explanation: Correct. 0x1A40 is `01 1010 0100 0000`: segment 01 (heap), offset 0xA40. 0xA40 < 0xC00, so the physical address is 0x9000 + 0xA40 = 0x9A40.

options.text: 0xAA40
options.explanation: This adds the whole virtual address (0x1A40) to the base. The segment bits must be stripped off first; only the 12-bit offset is added.
This uses the code segment's base. The top two bits are 01, which selects the heap.

options.text: Segmentation fault, offset out of range
options.explanation: The offset 0xA40 (2,624) is below the heap size 0xC00 (3,072), so the access is legal.

questions.workedExample:
1. Write 0x1A40 in binary: `0001 1010 0100 0000`.
2. Keep the low 14 bits: `01 1010 0100 0000`.
3. Top two bits `01` select the **heap**.
4. Low 12 bits `1010 0100 0000` = **0xA40** = 2,624.
5. Bounds check, then add the base:

```formula
seg = ⌊0x1A40 / 2^12⌋ = 1
off = 0x1A40 mod 2^12 = 0xA40
off = 2,624 < 3,072 = size_1
PA = base_1 + off
PA = 0x9000 + 0xA40 = 0x9A40
where
seg: the segment number, the top 2 bits of the 14-bit address; 1 (binary 01) is the heap
off: the offset inside the segment, the low 12 bits
2^12: 4,096 (0x1000); dividing by it removes the 12 offset bits
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after division
size_1: the heap segment's size, 0xC00 = 3,072 bytes
base_1: the heap segment's base, 0x9000
PA: the physical address
In words: 0x1A40 is 0xA40 bytes into the heap, which fits inside its 0xC00 bytes, so it lands at 0x9000 + 0xA40.
```

Notice the hex trick: with a 12-bit offset, the last three hex digits *are* the offset, and the leading digit 1 here means segment 01.

questions.prompt: A segmentation-based system has 512 MiB of RAM. After hours of running, free memory consists of holes of 30 MiB, 25 MiB and 40 MiB (95 MiB in total). A new process needs a single 60 MiB segment. What is the problem, and what would solve it?

options.text: Internal fragmentation; use smaller segments
options.explanation: Internal fragmentation is wasted space *inside* an allocated block. Here the waste is between allocations, which is external fragmentation.

options.text: Thrashing; add swap space
options.explanation: Thrashing is about constant paging when the working set doesn't fit. This is a placement problem: the total is enough, but not contiguous.

options.text: External fragmentation; compact memory by moving segments together, or switch to fixed-size paging
options.explanation: Correct. 95 MiB is free, but no hole is 60 MiB. Compaction can merge the holes (slowly, by copying), and paging avoids the problem since any free frame can hold any page.

options.text: The process is simply too big; there is not enough free memory
options.explanation: There *is* enough in total (95 MiB > 60 MiB). The issue is that it is split into pieces too small to hold a contiguous segment.

questions.workedExample:
1. Total free: 30 + 25 + 40 = 95 MiB, which exceeds the 60 MiB needed.
2. A segment must be contiguous in physical memory. The largest hole is 40 MiB, so the request fails.
3. Free space split into unusable pieces *between* allocations is **external fragmentation**.
4. Fixes:
   - **Compaction**: stop processes, copy their segments together, update base registers. This leaves one 95 MiB hole but costs a lot of copying.
   - **Paging**: split memory into fixed-size frames. A 60 MiB region becomes 15,360 pages of 4 KiB (60 × 1,024 KiB divided by 4 KiB) that can go in any free frames.

questions.prompt: 200 processes run the same program, whose code is 10 MiB. Under **base and bounds**, each process's code must sit inside its own contiguous region. Under **segmentation** with a shared, read-only code segment, all 200 can map the same physical copy. Roughly how much RAM does the code use in each case?

options.text: 10 MiB with base and bounds; 2,000 MiB with segmentation
options.explanation: This has the cases reversed. Sharing is what segmentation adds; base and bounds forces one copy per process.

options.text: 2,000 MiB in both, because each process needs its own copy
options.explanation: Read-only code never changes, so there is no reason for separate copies once the hardware can map one segment into many address spaces.

options.text: About 2,000 MiB with base and bounds; about 10 MiB with segmentation
options.explanation: Correct. Separate copies need 2,000 MiB in total, whereas the shared-code scheme needs one 10 MiB code copy plus per-process segment-table metadata.

options.text: 10 MiB in both, because the OS deduplicates pages automatically
options.explanation: Base and bounds has no way to point part of one address space at another region; its single base register covers the whole process.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Base and bounds**: one base register per process covers its *entire* address space, code included. So each process holds its own 10 MiB copy: 200 × 10 = **2,000 MiB**.
2. **Segmentation**: each segment has its own base. Every process's code-segment entry can point at the *same* physical base, with protection bits set to read and execute only so no process can modify it.
3. Cost: one 10 MiB copy plus a few bytes of segment-table entry per process, about **10 MiB**.
4. Paging does the same at page granularity, which is how Linux shares libc and executables today.

lessons.title: How x86 moved from segments to paging
lessons.summary: Real-mode segment arithmetic differs from protected-mode segment descriptors.
lessons.body:
### The x86 story

Intel's processors carry the history with them:

- The **8086** (1978) formed a 20-bit physical address from a 16-bit segment value and a 16-bit offset, mainly to reach 1 MiB with 16-bit registers:

```formula
PA = (16seg + off) mod 2^20
2^20 B = 1,048,576 B = 1 MiB
where
PA: the 20-bit physical address
seg: the 16-bit value in a segment register
off: the 16-bit offset within the segment
mod: the remainder after division; retaining only the low twenty bits here
2^20: 20 copies of 2 multiplied together, the number of addresses 20 bits can name
B: byte
MiB: mebibyte, 2^20 bytes
In words: shift the segment value left four bits, add the offset, and keep the low twenty bits. On the original 8086 a carry beyond 1 MiB wraps to the start.
```

For example, segment 0x1234 and offset 0x0010 select physical byte 0x12350. The original 8086 retains only the low twenty address bits, so a sum beyond 1 MiB wraps; later real-mode hardware can enable an additional address bit, so wrapping rules differ. Many segment/offset pairs name the same byte.

- The **80286** added protected mode with segment descriptors holding base, limit and privilege level.
- The **80386** added **paging** underneath segmentation, and later 32-bit Linux systems used largely flat ordinary code/data segments with paging for isolation. Special segments and early Linux designs were exceptions.
- In **native x86-64 64-bit mode** (not its 32-bit compatibility submode), the hardware ignores the base and limit of the CS, DS, ES and SS segments. Only FS and GS bases survive, and they are used for thread-local storage (glibc points FS at each thread's thread-local storage block).

For ordinary fixed-size page mappings, any suitable free frame can back a page. Physical fragmentation still matters for larger contiguous allocations, huge pages and device constraints. That is the subject of the next lesson.

## Where caches fit

CPU cache organization varies. A common design uses physical tags and a virtually indexed L1, allowing translation and cache-index lookup to overlap, but caches are a separate topic covered in the Computer Architecture subject. Here we care about the mapping, not about how fast RAM itself is.

## Key takeaways
- Real-mode segment arithmetic differs from protected-mode segment descriptors.
- Native 64-bit x86 largely ignores ordinary segment bases and limits, while FS and GS bases remain useful.
- Translation and CPU caches solve different problems.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: Which statements about segmentation on **x86-64 in 64-bit long mode** are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The base addresses of CS, DS, ES and SS are treated as 0
options.explanation: Correct. Long mode ignores these bases, giving a flat address space.

options.text: The FS and GS segment bases are still honoured, and are used for thread-local storage
options.explanation: Correct. glibc points FS at each thread's thread-local storage block, and the kernel uses GS for per-CPU data.

options.text: Segment limits are checked on every data access, so Linux uses them to isolate processes
options.explanation: Wrong. Long mode does not check limits for these segments, and Linux isolates processes with page tables, not segments.

options.text: Paging is optional in long mode; segmentation can be used instead
options.explanation: Wrong. Long mode *requires* paging to be enabled. Segmentation is vestigial.

questions.workedExample: 8086 real mode multiplied the segment value by 16 and added the offset, giving 20-bit addresses. The 286 added protected segmentation; the 386 added paging. Later 32-bit Linux largely used flat code/data segments, with exceptions. Native 64-bit mode ignores CS/DS/ES/SS bases and ordinary segment limits, while FS/GS bases remain useful for thread-local storage and per-CPU data. Compatibility mode has different segmentation semantics.

lessons.title: Pages, frames and unchanged offsets
lessons.summary: Translation replaces a virtual page number with a frame number and preserves the offset.
lessons.body:
Segmentation chopped memory into variable-sized pieces and paid for it with external fragmentation. **Paging** takes the opposite approach: chop *everything* into small, fixed-size blocks.

- The virtual address space is divided into **pages**.
- Physical memory is divided into **frames** (or page frames) of the same size.
- A **page table** records, for each virtual page, which physical frame holds it.

For a fixed base-page size, any suitable free frame can back a page; an ordinary virtual region need not occupy one physical hole. Physical contiguity still matters for huge pages and some device/kernel allocations. A process's pages can be scattered all over RAM while appearing perfectly contiguous to the program.

On x86-64 the standard page size is **4 KiB** (4,096 bytes), with optional huge pages of 2 MiB and 1 GiB.

## Splitting an address

Since a 4 KiB page contains 4,096 bytes, the low 12 bits of an address say where you are *inside* the page. The remaining high bits say *which* page.

```
 virtual address
 +------------------+------------+
 | virtual page no. |  offset    |
 |      (VPN)       |  12 bits   |
 +------------------+------------+
          | page table lookup
          v
 +------------------+------------+
 |  frame no. (PFN) |  offset    |
 +------------------+------------+
 physical address
```

Translation replaces the VPN with the PFN and keeps the offset unchanged. The offset never needs translating because a page and its frame have the same internal layout. As arithmetic, splitting is a division: the quotient is the page number and the remainder is the offset.

```formula
P = 2^k
VPN = ⌊VA / P⌋
off = VA mod P
PA = PFN P + off
where
P: the page size in bytes; 4 KiB = 4,096 on x86-64
k: the number of offset bits; 12 for 4 KiB pages, because 2^12 = 4,096
2^k: k copies of 2 multiplied together
VA: the virtual address
VPN: the virtual page number: which page the address falls in
off: the offset: how far into the page, from 0 to P − 1
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after division; for example 13 mod 5 = 3
PA: the physical address
PFN: the physical frame number: which frame holds the page, read from the page table entry for VPN
In words: divide the address by the page size; the quotient picks the page and the remainder is the position inside it. Translation swaps the page number for a frame number and keeps the remainder.
```

Because P is a power of two, the division needs no divider. The offset is simply the low k bits and the VPN is the bits above them, which is why the code below uses shifts (`>>`) and masks (`&`) instead.

> [!example] A toy translation
> A machine has 16-bit addresses and 4 KiB pages: 4 bits of VPN, 12 bits of offset, so 16 virtual pages. The page table says VPN 3 maps to PFN 7.

```formula
VPN = ⌊0x3A7C / 2^12⌋ = 0x3
off = 0x3A7C mod 2^12 = 0xA7C
PA = 0x7 × 2^12 + 0xA7C = 0x7A7C
where
VPN: the virtual page number; 0x3 maps to frame 0x7 in this page table
off: the offset inside the page
2^12: 4,096, which is 0x1000 in hexadecimal: one 4 KiB page
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after division
PA: the physical address
In words: 0x3A7C is 0xA7C bytes into page 3; page 3 lives in frame 7, so the byte is 0xA7C bytes into frame 7, at 0x7A7C.
```

With 4 KiB pages, multiplying or dividing by 4,096 (0x1000) moves hex digits, so the last three hex digits are always the offset. That makes hex translation quick by eye: replace the leading digits (the VPN) with the PFN.

Here is the same idea in Python:

```python
PAGE_BITS = 12
OFF_MASK = (1 << PAGE_BITS) - 1
# Sparse toy mappings: VPN to frame number.
page_table = {0: 5, 1: 9, 3: 7}

def translate(va):
    # High bits pick the page-table entry.
    vpn = va >> PAGE_BITS
    # The low offset bits stay unchanged.
    off = va & OFF_MASK
    if vpn not in page_table:
        raise MemoryError("page fault")
    pfn = page_table[vpn]
    # Place the frame above the offset bits.
    return (pfn << PAGE_BITS) | off

print(hex(translate(0x3A7C)))  # 0x7a7c
print(hex(translate(0x0123)))  # 0x5123
translate(0x2000)  # VPN 2: page fault
```

## Key takeaways
- Translation replaces a virtual page number with a frame number and preserves the offset.
- A power-of-two page size lets shifts and masks separate the fields.

## Further reading

- [OSTEP: Paging: Smaller Tables (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-smalltables.pdf)

- [x86_64 memory map — Linux kernel documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/arch/x86/x86_64/mm.html)

questions.prompt: A system uses 4 KiB pages. The page table maps **VPN 0x5 to PFN 0x12**. What physical address does virtual address **0x5ABC** translate to?

options.text: 0x5ABC
options.explanation: This forgets to translate at all: the page number must be replaced by the frame number.

options.text: 0x12ABC
options.explanation: Correct. The low twelve bits give offset 0xABC. Virtual page 0x5 maps to frame 0x12, so the physical address combines that frame with the unchanged offset.

options.text: 0x17ABC
options.explanation: This adds the PFN to the VPN (0x12 + 0x5 = 0x17). Paging *replaces* the page number; it does not add a base like base-and-bounds.

options.text: 0x120ABC
options.explanation: This shifts the PFN by 16 bits instead of 12. With 4 KiB pages the offset is 12 bits, i.e. exactly three hex digits.

questions.workedExample:
1. A 4 KiB page contains 4,096 bytes, requiring the low **12 bits** for its offset: three hex digits.
2. Address 0x5ABC selects virtual page 0x5 and offset 0xABC.
3. Look up VPN 0x5 → PFN 0x12.
4. Put the frame number above the offset:

```formula
PA = PFN × 2^12 + off
PA = 0x12 × 0x1000 + 0xABC
PA = 0x12000 + 0xABC = 0x12ABC
where
PA: the physical address
PFN: the physical frame number from the page table; here 0x12
2^12: 4,096, the page size, which is 0x1000 in hex
off: the offset inside the page, the low 12 bits of the virtual address; here 0xABC
In words: multiplying the frame number by 0x1000 appends three hex zeros, and the offset fills them in.
```

Shortcut: with 4 KiB pages, write the PFN and then append the last three hex digits of the virtual address.

questions.prompt: A system uses **16 KiB** pages and 48-bit virtual addresses. How many bits of each virtual address form the page offset, and how many form the virtual page number?

options.text: 12-bit offset, 36-bit VPN
options.explanation: Those are the numbers for 4 KiB pages. A 16 KiB page needs 2 more offset bits.

options.text: 16-bit offset, 32-bit VPN
options.explanation: Sixteen offset bits cover 65,536 bytes, so this is the split for 64 KiB pages.

options.text: 14-bit offset, 34-bit VPN
options.explanation: Correct. A 16 KiB page contains 16,384 bytes, requiring fourteen offset bits; the remaining thirty-four address bits identify its virtual page.

options.text: 14-bit offset, 48-bit VPN
options.explanation: The VPN is what is *left* after the offset: the two fields together make up the 48-bit address.

questions.workedExample:
The offset needs enough bits to number every byte in a page, and the page number gets whatever is left:

```formula
k = log_2(P) = log_2(16,384) = 14
v = n − k = 48 − 14 = 34
2^v × 2^k = 2^34 × 2^14 = 2^48
where
k: the number of offset bits
log_2: the base-2 logarithm: the power of 2 that gives the number; 2^14 = 16,384
P: the page size in bytes; 16 KiB = 16 × 1,024 = 16,384
v: the number of virtual-page-number (VPN) bits
n: the number of virtual-address bits, 48
2^v: the number of virtual pages
2^k: the bytes per page
In words: 14 bits pick a byte inside a 16 KiB page, the other 34 bits pick the page, and together they cover all 2^48 bytes.
```

16 KiB is a supported ARM64 translation granule; this question explicitly assumes a 48-bit virtual address width.

lessons.title: What page-table permission bits mean
lessons.summary: Page-table entries hold permissions and access state as well as a frame address.
lessons.body:
## What a page table entry holds

A **page table entry (PTE)** is more than a frame number. For ordinary x86-64 4 KiB leaf mappings, entries are 8 bytes. The table summarizes selected fields; implemented physical-address width and enabled CPU features constrain their interpretation:

| Bit(s) | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | P | Present: mapping valid |
| 1 | R/W | Writable |
| 2 | U/S | User mode may access |
| 5 | A | Accessed (set by CPU) |
| 6 | D | Dirty: page written |
| 8 | G | Global translation when enabled |
| 12–51 | PFN field | Address bits, limited by MAXPHYADDR |
| 63 | NX | No-execute |

The OS sets P, R/W, U/S and NX to express permissions. The CPU maintains **A** and **D** for translation use and writes. After clearing them, the OS must use the required invalidation protocol to observe later accesses reliably; cached translations do not promise a fresh in-memory bit update on every access. The OS reads those bits later to decide what to evict (the replacement units) and whether an evicted page must be written to disk first.

If P is 0, the hardware ignores the rest of the entry and raises a **page fault**. The OS can encode software state such as swap information in a non-present entry, while respecting architectural and security constraints. Non-present entries must not be treated as unconstrained storage on every implementation.

For ordinary user-mode accesses with NX support enabled and coherent translations, writing through a read-only mapping, reading a supervisor-only mapping, or executing an NX mapping faults. Supervisor write protection depends on control state; cached translations must be invalidated after changing permissions. This is how code is made read-only and data non-executable.

## Key takeaways
- Page-table entries hold permissions and access state as well as a frame address.
- Hardware permissions require coherent invalidation when software changes a mapping.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: For ordinary user-mode x86-64 accesses, with NX enabled and no stale cached translations, which conditions cause a page fault? Assume canonical addresses and all other permissions permit the access. Select all that apply.

options.text: Reading a page whose PTE has the Present bit clear
options.explanation: Correct. A non-present entry always faults; the kernel then decides whether to load the page or send SIGSEGV.

options.text: Writing to a page whose PTE has R/W clear
options.explanation: Correct. Write-protection violations fault. Copy-on-write relies on exactly this.

options.text: User-mode code reading a page whose PTE has U/S clear
options.explanation: Correct. Supervisor-only pages fault from user mode; this protects the kernel's mappings.

options.text: Reading a page whose Dirty bit is clear
options.explanation: Wrong. A clear dirty bit records no observed write since it was cleared; it is not a write-protection flag. Under the question’s permitted-access assumptions, hardware can set it during a write without causing this kind of page fault.

options.text: Executing code from a page with the NX bit set
options.explanation: Correct. Instruction fetches from no-execute pages fault, which blocks code injected into data or the stack.

questions.workedExample: In this model, non-present mappings, writes forbidden by R/W, user accesses forbidden by U/S and execution forbidden by NX fault. Clear A/D bits are bookkeeping state rather than a reason to reject an otherwise permitted access. Hardware-maintained A/D state and permission changes still require correct OS invalidation protocols; this is not a full specification of every paging mode.

lessons.title: Why a flat page table is too large
lessons.summary: A flat table needs an entry for every possible virtual page, including unused pages.
lessons.body:
## The size problem

A single flat array with one PTE per virtual page is simple, but consider its size. It needs one entry for every page the address space could hold, used or not:

```formula
E = 2^n / P
S = E × s_PTE
where
E: the number of entries in the flat table: one per virtual page
n: the number of virtual-address bits
2^n: the size of the virtual address space in bytes
P: the page size in bytes; 2^12 = 4,096 for 4 KiB pages
S: the size of the flat page table, per process, in bytes
s_PTE: the size of one page table entry (PTE) in bytes: 4 on 32-bit x86, 8 on x86-64
In words: count the pages in the address space, then multiply by the size of one entry.
```

Two cases with 4 KiB pages:

```formula
E_32 = 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20
S_32 = 2^20 × 4 B = 2^22 B = 4 MiB
E_48 = 2^48 / 2^12 = 2^36
S_48 = 2^36 × 8 B = 2^39 B = 512 GiB
where
E_32: entries for a 32-bit address space (about a million)
S_32: its flat-table size, with 4-byte entries
E_48: entries for a 48-bit address space (x86-64)
S_48: its flat-table size, with 8-byte entries
B: bytes
MiB: mebibyte, 2^20 bytes
GiB: gibibyte, 2^30 bytes
In words: dividing powers of two subtracts exponents and multiplying adds them; a flat table costs 4 MiB per process at 32 bits but 512 GiB at 48 bits.
```

- **32-bit**: **4 MiB per process**. Tolerable, but it adds up across hundreds of processes.
- **48-bit** (x86-64): **512 GiB** for the full 48-bit space. This is an impractical flat-table overhead for ordinary processes.

Yet a typical process uses only a few hundred MiB scattered across a 128 TiB space. Nearly all of the flat table would say "not present". The fix is to avoid storing those empty stretches.

## Key takeaways
- A flat table needs an entry for every possible virtual page, including unused pages.
- Address width, page size and entry size determine that overhead.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: A 32-bit system uses 4 KiB pages and a **single-level (flat)** page table with 4-byte entries. How large is each process's page table?

options.text: 4 KiB
options.explanation: That is one page, enough for 1,024 entries, which maps only 4 MiB of address space.

options.text: 1 MiB
options.explanation: This counts 1,048,576 entries as bytes, forgetting that every entry occupies four bytes.

options.text: 4 GiB
options.explanation: That is the size of the whole 32-bit address space, not of the table describing it.

options.text: 4 MiB
options.explanation: Correct. There are 1,048,576 virtual pages and four bytes per entry, requiring 4 MiB even when almost all pages are unused.

questions.workedExample:
A flat table has one entry for every possible virtual page, used or not:

```formula
E = 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 = 1,048,576
S = E × 4 B = 2^22 B = 4 MiB
where
E: the number of virtual pages, and so of table entries
2^32: the size of the 32-bit address space in bytes
2^12: the page size, 4,096 bytes (4 KiB)
S: the size of the flat page table
B: bytes; each entry is 4 bytes
MiB: mebibyte, 2^20 bytes
In words: about a million pages at 4 bytes each is 4 MiB per process, however little memory the process uses.
```

With 200 processes that is 800 MiB just for page tables, which is why even 32-bit x86 used a two-level table (a page directory of 1,024 entries pointing to page tables of 1,024 entries).

lessons.title: Building a sparse page-table tree
lessons.summary: A sparse tree avoids allocating lower tables for entirely unused regions.
lessons.body:
## Multi-level page tables

The trick is to **page the page table**. Split the VPN into several chunks and build a tree. The top-level table points to second-level tables, and so on. If an entire region is unused, the upper entry is simply marked not-present, and the tables below it are never allocated.

x86-64 uses a 4-level tree for 48-bit addresses. Each table is exactly one 4 KiB page holding 512 entries of 8 bytes, so each level consumes 9 bits of the address. The general rule for how many levels a tree needs:

```formula
e = P / s_PTE
b = log_2(e)
L = ⌈(n − k) / b⌉
e = 4,096 B / 8 B = 512
b = log_2(512) = 9
L = ⌈(48 − 12) / 9⌉ = 4
where
e: the number of entries in one table, when each table fills exactly one page
P: the page size; 4,096 bytes here
s_PTE: the size of one entry; 8 bytes on x86-64
b: the address bits each level consumes: the bits needed to pick one of e entries
log_2: the base-2 logarithm: the power you raise 2 to in order to get the number; 2^9 = 512, so log_2(512) = 9
L: the number of levels in the tree
n: the number of virtual-address bits translated; 48 here
k: the number of offset bits; 12 for 4 KiB pages
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to a whole number (a part-used level is still a level)
B: bytes
In words: a page-sized table of 8-byte entries holds 512 of them, so each level picks one of 512 using 9 bits, and the 36 page-number bits need 4 levels.
```

The 48 bits split like this:

```
47   39 38   30 29   21 20   12 11     0
+------+------+------+------+--------+
| PML4 | PDPT |  PD  |  PT  | offset |
|  9   |  9   |  9   |  9   |   12   |
+------+------+------+------+--------+
```

9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 12 = 48 bits. Bits 63 to 48 must be copies of bit 47 (the canonical-address rule).

| Intel name | Linux name | One entry covers |
|---|---|---|
| PML4 | PGD (P4D folded) | 512 GiB |
| PDPT | PUD | 1 GiB |
| PD | PMD | 2 MiB |
| PT | PTE | 4 KiB |

Each level up multiplies the coverage by 512, because one entry points at a whole table of 512 entries below it:

```formula
C_PT = 4 KiB
C_PD = 512 × 4 KiB = 2 MiB
C_PDPT = 512 × 2 MiB = 1 GiB
C_PML4 = 512 × 1 GiB = 512 GiB
where
C_PT: the memory one PT entry maps: one 4 KiB page
C_PD: the memory one PD entry covers: a whole PT's worth of pages
C_PDPT: the memory one PDPT entry covers
C_PML4: the memory one PML4 entry covers
KiB: kibibyte, 1,024 bytes
MiB: mebibyte, 1,024 KiB
GiB: gibibyte, 1,024 MiB
In words: 512 × 4 KiB is 2 MiB, 512 × 2 MiB is 1 GiB, and 512 × 1 GiB is 512 GiB, so one top-level entry spans half a tebibyte.
```

The physical address of the top-level table lives in the **CR3** register. A context switch to another process loads its CR3 value, and that one register write switches the whole address space.

## Key takeaways
- A sparse tree avoids allocating lower tables for entirely unused regions.
- Four 9-bit indices and a 12-bit offset cover a 48-bit address.
- CR3 identifies the active x86 page-table root.

questions.prompt: Suppose an architecture uses **64 KiB pages** and 8-byte page table entries, with each table occupying exactly one page. How many levels are needed to translate a **48-bit** virtual address?

options.explanation: Two levels of 13 bits plus a 16-bit offset covers only 42 bits, 6 short of 48.

Correct. A 64 KiB page needs sixteen offset bits. Its 8,192 table entries need thirteen index bits per level. Thirty-two page-number bits therefore need three levels, with the top level partly used. The worked formula shows the ceiling calculation.
Four levels is the x86-64 answer for 4 KiB pages (9 bits per level). Larger pages mean both a bigger offset and more bits per level.
Five levels is x86-64 with 57-bit addresses and 4 KiB pages.

questions.workedExample:
Find the offset size, the bits each table resolves, then how many tables the remaining bits need:

```formula
k = log_2(P) = log_2(65,536) = 16
e = P / s_PTE = 65,536 / 8 = 8,192
b = log_2(e) = log_2(8,192) = 13
L = ⌈(n − k) / b⌉ = ⌈(48 − 16) / 13⌉
L = 3
where
k: the number of offset bits
log_2: the base-2 logarithm: the power of 2 that gives the number (2^16 = 65,536, 2^13 = 8,192)
P: the page size in bytes; 64 KiB = 65,536
e: the entries in one table, which fills one page
s_PTE: the size of one page table entry, 8 bytes
b: the address bits each level resolves
L: the number of levels
n: the number of virtual-address bits, 48
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to a whole number
In words: 16 offset bits leave 32 page-number bits, and at 13 bits per level that takes 3 levels, the top one only partly used.
```

The top level uses only 32 − 26 = 6 bits.

This matches ARM64 with the 64 KiB granule, which uses 3 levels for 48-bit addresses (and 2 levels for 42-bit). Bigger pages mean shallower trees and fewer memory accesses per TLB miss, at the cost of more internal fragmentation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about multi-level page tables are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: They save memory when the address space is sparse, because unused regions need no lower-level tables
options.explanation: Correct. A not-present upper entry stands in for a whole 512 GiB, 1 GiB or 2 MiB region.

options.text: An uncached multi-level walk to a base-page leaf requires more entry reads than a flat-table lookup
options.explanation: Correct. A flat table needs one PTE read; a 4-level tree needs four. That is the price of the space saving.

options.text: If every virtual page were mapped, the tree would use slightly more memory than a flat table
options.explanation: Correct. The leaf tables equal the flat table in total, and the upper levels add a little on top.

options.text: They eliminate internal fragmentation
options.explanation: Wrong. Internal fragmentation comes from rounding allocations up to whole pages, which is unaffected by how the page table is organised.

questions.workedExample: Sparse mappings can omit entire lower-level subtrees, with overhead depending on their address distribution. An uncached base-page walk reads one entry per level; paging-structure caches and huge leaves reduce that work. A fully populated tree uses the flat table's worth of leaf entries plus upper tables. Page-granularity allocation can still waste space; lazy allocation or suballocation changes actual resident usage.

questions.prompt: The scheduler switches from process A to process B, which have different userspace memory contexts, on x86-64. What does the kernel do so that the hardware starts translating with B's address space?

options.text: Copies B's page tables into a fixed kernel location that the MMU always reads
options.explanation: There is no fixed location: the MMU reads whatever tree CR3 points to, so copying would be pointless and very slow.

options.text: Rewrites every PTE in the shared page table to point to B's frames
options.explanation: Each process has its own tree. Rewriting entries would cost time proportional to B's memory on every switch.

options.text: Swaps A's memory out to disk and B's back in
options.explanation: Both processes can be resident at once; paging to disk is unrelated to a context switch.

options.text: Loads the physical address of B's top-level table into CR3
options.explanation: Correct. One register write switches the whole address space. Without PCIDs this also flushes non-global TLB entries; the later translation-cache units cover PCID retention and invalidation rules.

questions.workedExample: CR3 selects the physical page-table root and, when enabled, a PCID. Switching memory contexts requires selecting the appropriate root and maintaining TLB coherence; details include PCID/no-flush rules and KPTI. Tasks sharing the same memory context need no root change solely because their task identity changed. PCIDs permit retaining tagged translations only when the kernel also obeys invalidation/reuse rules.

lessons.title: Walking an x86 address bit by bit
lessons.summary: Extract one index per level, then combine the final frame with the unchanged offset.
lessons.body:
### A walk, bit by bit

Translate the virtual address **0x7ffd4a3b2c18** (a typical stack address). Each table index is a 9-bit field, found by shifting the address right past everything below the field (dividing by a power of two) and keeping 9 bits (the remainder after dividing by 512):

```formula
i = ⌊VA / 2^s⌋ mod 512
i_PML4 = ⌊VA / 2^39⌋ mod 512 = 255
i_PDPT = ⌊VA / 2^30⌋ mod 512 = 501
i_PD = ⌊VA / 2^21⌋ mod 512 = 81
i_PT = ⌊VA / 2^12⌋ mod 512 = 434
off = VA mod 2^12 = 0xc18 = 3,096
where
i: the index into one level's table, from 0 to 511
VA: the virtual address, here 0x7ffd4a3b2c18
s: the bit position where that level's field starts: 39, 30, 21 or 12
2^s: s copies of 2 multiplied together; dividing by it discards the s bits below the field
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after division; mod 512 keeps the lowest 9 bits, because 512 = 2^9
i_PML4: the index into the top-level PML4 table
i_PDPT: the index into the PDPT
i_PD: the index into the PD
i_PT: the index into the PT
off: the 12-bit offset inside the final 4 KiB page
In words: cut the 48 bits into four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset; these are the numbers the MMU uses at each level.
```

By hand, write the 48 bits in binary and cut them into fields:

```
0x7ffd4a3b2c18 =
011111111 111110101 001010001
110110010 110000011000

PML4: 011111111   (255)
PDPT: 111110101   (501)
PD:   001010001   (81)
PT:   110110010   (434)
off:  110000011000 (0xc18)
```

The same split in code:

```python
def split(va):
    # Keep the offset, then extract 9-bit
    # indices from leaf towards root.
    off  =  va        & 0xFFF
    pt   = (va >> 12) & 0x1FF
    pd   = (va >> 21) & 0x1FF
    pdpt = (va >> 30) & 0x1FF
    pml4 = (va >> 39) & 0x1FF
    return pml4, pdpt, pd, pt, off

print(split(0x7ffd4a3b2c18))
# (255, 501, 81, 434, 3096)
```

(3,096 is hexadecimal 0xc18. In the code, `va >> s` discards the low bits selected by the shift amount and `& 0x1FF` keeps the next nine bits.) Now the MMU walks the tree:

```
CR3 -> PML4 table
       entry 255 -> PDPT table
         entry 501 -> PD table
           entry 81 -> PT table
             entry 434 -> PFN 0x1a2b3
```

After the walk, combine the final frame and offset using the same rule as before:

```formula
PA = PFN × 2^12 + off
PA = 0x1a2b3 × 0x1000 + 0xc18
PA = 0x1a2b3c18
where
PA: the physical address
PFN: the physical frame number from the PT entry; here 0x1a2b3
2^12: 4,096 (0x1000), the page size; multiplying by it appends three hex zeros
off: the offset inside the page; here 0xc18
In words: the frame number supplies everything above the low 12 bits, and the unchanged offset fills the low 12 bits.
```

At each level the hardware reads one 8-byte entry, checks the present and permission bits, and takes the next table's physical address from bits 12 to 51. If any level's entry is not present, the walk stops with a page fault.

> [!warning] Four extra memory reads
> A naive walk costs **four memory accesses** before the real one, five total reads per data access in a serial, equally costly read model. This is a read-count model, not a universal latency multiplier. The TLB (next lesson) caches finished translations so that most accesses skip the walk entirely.

## Key takeaways
- Extract one index per level, then combine the final frame with the unchanged offset.
- An uncached four-level walk reads four entries before accessing the data.

options.text: PML4 0, PDPT 256, PD 256, PT 291, offset 0x456
options.explanation: Correct. Shift and mask 9 bits at a time: bits 47–39 = 0, 38–30 = 256, 29–21 = 256, 20–12 = 291 (0x123), and the low 12 bits are 0x456.

options.text: PML4 0, PDPT 1, PD 1, PT 0x123, offset 0x456
options.explanation: This reads the hex digits as if each level were a 4-bit or 8-bit field. Each level is 9 bits, which does not line up with hex digits.

options.explanation: This assigns bit 38 to the PML4 field. The PML4 index is bits 47 to 39, all of which are 0 here.

options.text: PML4 0, PDPT 256, PD 256, PT 291, offset 0x3456
options.explanation: The offset is only 12 bits (three hex digits); the 0x3 belongs to the PT index.

questions.workedExample:
Each index is a 9-bit field: divide by 2 to the power of the field's starting bit, then keep the remainder after dividing by 512:

```formula
i = ⌊VA / 2^s⌋ mod 512
i_PML4 = ⌊VA / 2^39⌋ mod 512 = 0
i_PDPT = ⌊VA / 2^30⌋ mod 512 = 256
i_PD = ⌊VA / 2^21⌋ mod 512 = 256
i_PT = ⌊VA / 2^12⌋ mod 512 = 291
off = VA mod 2^12 = 0x456
where
i: one level's table index, from 0 to 511
VA: the virtual address, 0x4020123456
s: the bit where that level's field starts: 39, 30, 21 or 12
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to a whole number
mod: the remainder after division; mod 512 keeps 9 bits
i_PML4: the PML4 index (bits 47 to 39)
i_PDPT: the PDPT index (bits 38 to 30)
i_PD: the PD index (bits 29 to 21)
i_PT: the PT index (bits 20 to 12); 291 is 0x123
off: the 12-bit page offset
In words: shift the address down past each field and keep 9 bits to get the four indices; the low 12 bits are the offset.
```

In code this is `(va >> s) & 0x1FF`: the shift discards the selected low bits, and masking keeps the next nine.

Check one: divide the address by 1,073,741,824 and round down. The result is 256, already below the 512-entry table size, so the PDPT index is 256.

In binary, the set bit at position 38 becomes bit eight of the PDPT index; the bit at position 29 becomes bit eight of the PD index. Each contributes 256.

questions.prompt: A single load stays within a present 4 KiB page on x86-64 with four-level paging. It misses all translation and page-walk caches. Count one read per paging level plus the data read, ignoring accessed-bit updates, nested virtualization and data-cache effects. How many reads does this model require?

options.explanation: That would only be true on a TLB hit, when the translation is already cached.
Four accesses are needed for the walk, but the load itself still has to read the data afterwards.
Correct. One read from each of the PML4, PDPT, PD and PT tables, then the actual data access.
That is the cost with a single-level page table: one PTE read plus the data.

questions.workedExample: Read PML4, PDPT, PD and PT entries, then the requested data: five reads in this simplified model. It is not a prediction of 5× wall-clock latency: cache hits, overlapping work and other hardware behavior matter. A five-level full walk adds one entry read.

lessons.title: Counting table pages and fragmentation
lessons.summary: Table cost depends on the distribution and density of populated addresses.
lessons.body:
### How much space does it save?

Imagine a small process whose code and heap sit in one 2 MiB region near the bottom of the address space and whose stack sits near the top.

- 1 PML4 table (always needed).
- Code and heap: 1 PDPT, 1 PD, 1 PT.
- Stack: a different PML4 entry, so its own PDPT, PD and PT.

That is 7 tables × 4 KiB = **28 KiB** of page tables, against 512 GiB for a flat table. Ignoring kernel mappings, KPTI and other process regions, this toy count assumes the stack also fits within one 2 MiB region. Table cost depends on mapped address distribution as well as size. For a densely mapped region, the leaf tables dominate:

```formula
S_PT = ⌈M / C_PD⌉ × 4 KiB
o = 4 KiB / 2 MiB = 4 / 2,048 ≈ 0.2 %
where
S_PT: the memory used by leaf page tables (PTs) for the region
M: the size of a densely mapped region beginning on a 2 MiB boundary
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up so a partly used leaf table still occupies a whole table page
C_PD: the memory one full PT maps, 2 MiB (512 entries × 4 KiB)
KiB: kibibyte, 1,024 bytes; each PT is one 4 KiB page
MiB: mebibyte, 1,024 KiB
o: the overhead: page-table bytes per mapped byte
≈: approximately equal to
%: per cent, hundredths
In words: every 2 MiB of densely mapped memory needs one 4 KiB leaf table, about 0.2 % extra; the upper levels add a little more.
```

## Trade-offs and pitfalls

- **Internal fragmentation.** Memory is handed out in whole pages. An independently backed 1-byte region can occupy a whole base page once allocated. Average half-page waste assumes roughly uniform allocation remainders; sharing, lazy allocation and suballocation change the result. Bigger pages can increase waste.
- **Page tables cost real memory.** A dense, populated 100 GiB mapping with 4 KiB pages needs 51,200 leaf page tables (100 GiB divided by the 2 MiB each one maps), and 51,200 × 4 KiB is about 200 MiB. Many processes sharing a large mapping each pay that separately, which is one reason big databases use huge pages.
- **Don't confuse page-aligned with frame-contiguous.** Two adjacent virtual pages can be in frames gigabytes apart. DMA mappings must meet the device's requirements; options include scatter/gather lists, IOMMU translation or physically contiguous buffers.

## Key takeaways
- Table cost depends on the distribution and density of populated addresses.
- Dense mappings pay mostly for leaf tables, while isolated regions need separate upper paths.
- Virtual alignment does not guarantee physical contiguity.
